title: Cycle-of-Science: Reliable Reasoning through Counterfactual Verification for Agent Decision Making
one_liner: Make an agent test candidate explanations against alternative possible outcomes before it commits to the next action.
lead: Agents often learn from experience by copying what seemed to work before. That can go wrong because repeated coincidence may look like true cause. An agent may keep choosing an action only because that action often appeared next to success, not because the action actually created success. This paper studies an agent loop that forms a hypothesis, tests alternatives, and validates the result before choosing the next step.

problem.h2: Agents confuse repeated correlation with actual cause
paras: A decision-making agent often sees many past episodes where a certain action and a good result appeared together. But that does not prove the action caused the good result. The good result may have depended on a hidden condition that happened to be present at the same time.

If the agent trains on such passive experience alone, it may adopt brittle rules. Those rules fail when the surrounding context changes because the agent never checked which factors really drive the outcome. The paper asks whether an agent can do something closer to hypothesis testing before it decides.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Make the agent test a candidate explanation against alternate possible cases before acting, because verified cause is a safer guide than repeated coincidence.

panels.title: 1. The agent sees a past pattern
panels.viz_args: Action A often appeared before a good result.
panels.caption: A repeated pattern looks persuasive even when the true cause is still unclear.

panels.title: 2. A hypothesis is proposed
panels.viz_args: Maybe Action A caused the good result.
panels.caption: This is only a guess, so the method does not trust it yet.

panels.title: 3. Alternate cases are checked
panels.caption: The system examines what would happen under changed conditions because that can separate cause from coincidence.

panels.title: 4. Weak explanations are discarded
panels.viz_args: Only explanations that survive the tests remain.
panels.caption: The agent removes flimsy stories because acting on them would repeat old mistakes.

panels.title: 5. The next action uses validated reasoning
panels.viz_args: Decision making is guided by the explanations that survived testing.
panels.caption: The goal is steadier action selection because the chosen reasons have been checked.

steps.text: Use available causal hints to propose why a certain action might help on the current task because the later tests need an explicit candidate explanation to check.
Change parts of the situation and inspect what the result would be so that the agent can tell whether the proposed cause still matters.
Measure how much the result changes when the hypothesized cause is changed because real causes should move the outcome in a consistent direction.
Retain only the explanations that survive the tests so that later decisions rely on stronger evidence.
Use the better-tested reasoning chains as training targets because the policy should prefer decisions backed by checked explanations.

paras: The paper changes the source of supervision for agent reasoning. Instead of rewarding whatever chain happened to precede success, it rewards chains that remain plausible after alternate-case testing.
object.object: the training signal for agent reasoning quality

hidden.name: how much the proposed reason would still matter if the surrounding situation changed
paras: The hidden quantity is causal stability. A proposed reason is stable if the result still changes when that reason changes, even after other conditions are varied. That quantity is not directly visible in one ordinary episode.

The method estimates it by checking alternate possible cases. This matters because a true cause should keep mattering across those checks, while a coincidental pattern should fade once the surrounding details are altered.

heat.caption: The method focuses on how the outcome changes under altered conditions, because that is where cause reveals itself most clearly.

reads.html: A reason is trustworthy if it still matters after you change the surrounding details.
Counterfactual verification estimates whether a candidate explanation carries real intervention effect, which means the agent can train on reasons that survive explicit testing.

mechanism.h2: Why the cycle can improve decisions
paras: Passive replay of past experience is weak when many events happen together. The agent may copy a pattern that is easy to see but causally empty. Explicit testing can help because it forces the policy to ask what would change if the proposed cause were altered.

The training stage also matters. If validated reasoning chains are preferred during learning, later decisions become more dependable because the agent is repeatedly pushed toward explanations that survived the hypothesis-experiment-validation loop.

stages.s: Measure whether the outcome changes in line with the hypothesis
Agent decisions backed by checked explanations

math.h2: A compact view of the test
math.words: The value of a proposed reason can be viewed as the difference between the outcome when that reason is present and the outcome when it is removed under a matched alternate case, because cause should change the result.
symbols: estimated effect of the proposed reason on the result
result when the hypothesized cause is present in the alternate case
result when that cause is removed or changed

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the agent thinks a retrieval step is why a task succeeds.
In a matched alternate case with the retrieval step kept, the outcome score is 8.
In a matched alternate case with that step removed, the outcome score is 3.
Then causal value is 5, which suggests the step matters.
If the two scores were nearly equal, the explanation would look weak because changing the supposed cause would barely affect the result.

math.note: The full paper uses a richer decision and training pipeline, but this difference captures the basic test for whether a candidate reason moves the outcome.

bars.h2: What the experiments are trying to show

charts.title: Passive experience learning
charts.note: A weak baseline tends to retain attractive but untested stories because it learns only from ordinary co-occurrence.

charts.title: Cycle-of-Science training
charts.note: The desired pattern is better choices under changed conditions because the reasons behind those choices were explicitly tested.

items.b: Bad alternate cases can mislead the test.
items.html: If the alternate case changes too many things at once, the measured effect becomes hard to interpret because the supposed cause is no longer isolated.

items.b: The initial hypothesis can already be biased.
items.html: If the proposed explanation starts from a poor assumption, the loop may spend effort testing the wrong question because it never explored a better hypothesis.
The cycle adds computation before acting, so an urgent task may suffer because the agent cannot afford many validation steps.
The approach is strongest when false correlation is a common failure source, because then explicit alternate-case testing removes a major source of bad decisions.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a decision task where some action often appears near success but only helps under a hidden condition, so that the benchmark can separate real cause from coincidence. Let one agent learn from passive episodes and let another use the hypothesis-experiment-validation loop. During evaluation, shift the hidden condition across tasks.
The demo should show that the tested-reason agent makes fewer bad transfers because it learns which actions actually drive success instead of which actions merely appear beside success.
demo.metric_eq: causal_gain = false_stories_before - false_stories_after ; decision_gain = accuracy_after - accuracy_before
demo.closing: The point of the demo is to show that explicit verification helps because it separates cause from coincidence before the agent commits to a decision.
